about the technical part of data

sensitive. That means not only making a
bad decision in big topic like how to
module the data in star schema,
snowflake and so on could lead to bad
performance and bad results. As well, a
tiny small mistake that you decide in
the data model like for example, the
cardinality on a relationship between
two tables could lead to bad numbers and
bad results. So, that's why it is not an
easy topic to learn and to be honest to
teach. You have to do a lot of projects
in order to understand the different
scenarios and why we do those decisions.
Now, I'm going to do my best to bring
all the scenarios that I had in my
projects as a scenarios in this course.
So now, let's get started.
>> [groaning]
>> All right. So now, let's start with the
foundations. In Power BI, we have all
those different layers and we going to
focus now into two layers together, the
module and the visual layer. So, let's
zoom in. The visual layer, it is the
place where you going to go and build
your reports. So, usually you have like
maybe two tables and you pick one of
them and start drag and drop to the
visual to build maybe a table or a
chart, a card and Power BI going to just
show the visual. But now, what going to
happen if you go to another table and
drag and drop inside the same visual?
Now, Power BI going to say, "Okay, but
wait. How I'm going to go and combine
those two different data from two
different tables in one visual?" So,
Power BI need from you more infos in
order to combine the data and we cannot
define the logic in the visual layer. We
have to do it in the engine, in the
previous layer, the module layer. There,
we going to define everything, the shape
of the tables, how the tables are
related to each others using
relationships, the cardinality, the
filtering, the calculations, how the
data going to move from one table to
another, define the security rules. So,
Power BI going to find all the rules,
all the description about how everything
is related to each others and how
PowerBI going to go and deal with those
two informations in the visual. And
based of all those informations in the
module layer, PowerBI going to have all
the knowledge in order to calculate the
numbers and plot charts in the visual
layer. And here is the most important
thing to understand, if the numbers are
wrong in the visual layer, it is highly
likely because the rules, the shapes,
the relationships on the module layers
are wrong. So, bad model going to define
bad rules that going to lead to bad
numbers. And of course, my friends,
don't expect if you make mistakes on the
module layer that you going to find big
error message in the visual in the
reports. No, mostly the report going to
function, you going to see numbers, your
visuals are working, everything is okay.
Only if you or your users make zoom in
and start really checking the numbers,
they might start seeing those wrong
numbers. So, mostly the mistakes going
to lead to silent errors that it is
really hard to find. But, don't worry
about it, we're going to start with the
foundations. Now, it always starts like
this. In my data, I have two tables,
left and right, and I'm going to need
both of them in my reports. And here, my
friend, you have two options, not only
one. Either you're going to go and
combine those two tables together into
one single table, like we have done in
Power Query by merging the tables into
one, they are physically now one table,
or the other option that you say, "You
know what? Let's just leave them as it
is." So, we will not go to Power Query
and do anything. We will just like put a
line, a relationship between those two.
Physically, they going to start
separated from each others, but they
have a relationship between them. So,
this is the first decision that you have
to make, either in Power Query you are
merging or building relationships in the
module layer. Now, of course, we are
focusing on the relationships. So, what
are they? A relationship, it is like a
contract between two tables in order for
you to define the rules that going to
tell Power BI how to filter and how to
combine the data from those two tables
into one visual in the front end. And
now you might say, "Wait, wait. You said
relationships we don't combine data,
only merging in Power Query we combine."
So now we are combining actually in
relationships. So what is going on? What
is going on? Now let's zoom out again.
The three layers, Power Query, module
layer, and visual layer. Now if you
merge two tables, it going to happen at
the beginning in the start in the Power
Query. So everything going to be merged
together, the columns, the rows into one
single table. And of course in the next
layers, the module, the visual, you
going to see only one single table. So
that means combining the data happens in
very early stage in the Power Query. But
now in the other side, if you go to the
module layer and build a relationship
between those two tables, they will not
get combined. They going to stay
separated. So that means in module and
as well in visual layer, you going to
see the original two tables, but only if
you go and build a chart, a visual in
the visual layer, and you start picking
data from left and right, only there the
data going to get combined. And of
course not all columns, not all rows.
This depends on what you picked and what
filters you are using. Now of course you
going to say, "Okay, when we combine in
Power Query and when we build the
relationships?" The rule is very simple.
If two tables are describing the same
row, like for example you have customer
info and customer emails separated in
two different tables, then no need to
build a relationships, just go and
combine them at early stage in the Power
Query. But if you have two different
tables, like for example the sales and
the customers, it would be bad idea to
go and combine them together, instead
build a relationship between them. Those
are the two options and the first
decision that you have to make. But now
we have more things. Now in order to
build a relationship between two tables,
you have to define for Power BI three
things. First, you have to define the
keys. They are common columns between
two tables, like IDs, keys, or whatever,
so that Power BI know how to match the
rows between those two tables. Without
it, Power BI has no idea how to combine
the rows. Another thing you have to
define the cardinality. Yes, a fancy
name. So, you have to describe the
values inside those keys. And here we
have two options that we have to define
for each side. It is very simple. One
means the values are unique. There is no
repetitions. And other value, many,
means the values are repeating. They are
not unique, and one value can appear
multiple times. So, that means we have
two options, two sides. That means we
have four cardinality options. Yes, I
can do math.
>> Hey Michael, what's 394 * 5,912?
>> Let's see.
>> We have one to one, one to many, many to
one, and the evil and the one, the only,
many to many relationship. This going to
be the real suffer. Okay, so let's have
a very simple example. We start with the
one to one relationship. So, here we
have two tables about their customers.
One has the names, the other has the
tiers. And they are connected using the
customer ID. Now, let's go and check the
values inside the keys. We can see on
the left side, the keys are unique. For
each customer, we have exactly one row.
That's why the relationship on the left
side is one. Now, let's go and check the
right side. We have the exact same
thing. Values of the customer ID is
unique. There are no duplicates, and as
well on the right side it's going to be
one. So, that's it. This is the one to
one relationship. Now, let's have an
example about the one to many
relationship. So, on the left side we
have the customers again, and on the
right side we have the orders. Now, same
thing. We're going to check the values
inside the keys. On the customers, we
don't have duplicates, so they are all
unique. But, on the right side, we have
duplicates. So, for the first customer,
Maria did place two orders. So, on the
left side it is one, on the right side
it is many. It exist more than once.
Let's try out John. Same thing. On the
left side one, on the right side many.
But, of course, this is not must like
for example Anna, she ordered only once.
But since we have duplicates from other
customers, this relationship going to be
one to many. Now the many to one it's
exactly the same, but we just like flip.
So if the dimension now on the right
side we can say it is many to one
relationship. So the same thing we are
just like flipping the sides, nothing
new. Okay, now we come to the many to
many relationship and here we have two
tables. On the left side we have the
customer segments and on the right side
we have the orders, the sales. Same
thing, they are connected using the
customer ID. But now if you have a look
to this you can see the customer ID is
not anymore unique on the left side. So
a customer could belong to multiple
segments. And on the right side the fact
it was normal because a customer could
order multiple things. So that means if
I click to one of those customers, same
effect, they go and like order multiple
things. But now here is the issue, one
order belongs now to two rows on the
left side because the customer belong to
two segments. So that means that left
side is not anymore one. It is many and
with that we have many to many
relationship. So we have to define the
rules or the cardinality. Another thing
that you have to define is the filter
direction. Now in reporting we filter
data like crazy and we have to define
the direction of how the filter going to
move from one table to another and
whether it is allowed. And in order to
control the traffic of the filters, we
have as well some options. So now again
we have this simple example where we
have two tables, the sales and the
segments. And for each table we have
like an aggregation. For the segments we
have the total number of segments and
here we have the total number of sales.
Now one option to define the direction
of the filters to say it is single
filter from the left to the right. So
for example if I go and filter the data
for the customer ID, you can see the
sales is already filtered with the
total, but as well the right side is
filtered. So we have here only two
segments. Same thing, if I go and filter
the data by another customer, you can
see it always has an effect on the right
side. So, whatever I'm filtering on the
left, the filter is going to the right
side. But now, if I go and start
filtering from the right side, you can
see, okay, the table is filtered, we
have only two segments, but this filter
has no effect on the sales. I'm still
seeing the total number of sales. So,
the filter is not traveling from the
right side to the left side. Same thing
if I go and select the other customers.
You can see, the sales table is not
affected. Now, of course, we can do the
opposite where we can say single filter
from segment to the sales. So, this time
if I filter on the segments, it going to
filter the sales. But now, of course, if
I filter the sales, there's no effect on
the right side. Now, if you say, you
know what, let's have it free for all.
Everything filter everything. For that,
we're going to use the both. So, that
means if I'm filtering on the left side,
the data going to get filtered on the
right side, and the same thing if I'm
filtering on the right side, the data
are getting filtered on the left side.
So, wherever I'm filtering, it going to
go everywhere. So, as you can see, my
friends, with this we can control the
behavior of the whole data model, how
the data is filtered, and this has a
great effect on the reports. So, those
are the three rules that we have to
define on the relationships, the keys,
cardinalities, and the filter direction.
And guess what, we will not do this only
between two tables, we have to do it for
the whole data model. Each time you
connect two tables, you have to define
those, and if you do it wrong, you're
going to get wrong results. All right,
my friends, so now enough with the
sketches and the theory, let's go back
to Power BI and practice.
